sections.description: Also known as Shortest Remaining Time First (SRTF). If multiple processes arrive together or are in the ready queue, the process with the smallest remaining burst time is executed first. If burst times are the same, the one with the earliest arrival time is chosen.
rules: Preemptive execution: Checks ready queue continuously or when a new process arrives.
If burst time is identical, select the process with the lower arrival time.

sections.description: Each process is assigned a numerical priority. The CPU is allocated to the process with the highest priority.
sections.Note on Numerical Priority: Highest priority can mean highest importance or vice-versa based on problem context. If priority numbers are identical, resolve using arrival time (lower arrival time gets preference).

types.description: If a newly arrived process has a higher priority than the currently running process, the current process is preempted.
Once a process starts execution, it runs to completion regardless of newly arriving higher-priority processes.

drawbacks.description: Low-priority processes may never get the CPU if high-priority processes continually arrive.
As time progresses, incrementally increase the priority of waiting processes so they eventually execute.

sections.description: Similar to FCFS, but designed with preemption using a fixed time quantum.
rules: Each process gets a small unit of CPU time (Time Quantum).
If the process's burst time exceeds the quantum, it is preempted and added to the end of the ready queue.
Provides fair allocation of CPU time to all processes.

sections.title: Context Switch
sections.definition: The mechanism where the system saves the state (context) of the old process and loads the saved state for the new process via the Process Control Block (PCB).
characteristics: Context-switch time is pure system overhead; the system performs no useful user work while switching.
Complexity depends on hardware support (e.g., multiple sets of registers).

preemptive: A running process can be interrupted and forced to leave the CPU.
non_preemptive: Once a process starts execution, it cannot be interrupted until it finishes.
May cause longer waiting times for short processes (e.g., Convoy Effect).

comparisons.convoy_effect: Short processes wait for a long process to finish execution. Commonly occurs in FCFS scheduling.
comparisons.starvation: A process waits for an indefinitely long time because other processes continuously get priority or CPU access. Commonly occurs in Priority Scheduling.

sections.title: CPU Utilization
sections.definition: CPU utilization refers to the percentage of time the CPU remains busy executing processes.
sections.example_explanation: If an algorithm has 60% CPU utilization, it means the CPU spends 60% of its time working/busy and 40% of its time idle.

problems.details: Involves threads/processes ($P_1$ to $P_6$) with priorities, burst times, arrival times, an idle task ($P_0$ priority 0), and a time quantum of 10 units.
Scheduler executes highest-priority processes; for matching priorities, uses Round-Robin with a time quantum of 10 units.
